And the final phrase expresses the full seriousness of the
decision: "Blessed is he who takes no offence at me." It is
therefore clear that if Jesus is the One who is to come, He
is not so in the plain unequivocal way which longings and
hopes, desires and fancies picture. He is not so in the sense
which men imagine that He must be. That He should be the
One who is to come is an astonishing fact, and for many
repulsive and offensive. As to whether He truly is the One
who is to come, the burden of decision rests on us.
But secondly, there must have been a certain state of
affairs with regard to Him, arousing a certain reaction
towards Him, so that the grounds for a considered judgment
were there. And what is this state of affairs? The picture is
suggested in the words: "The blind see." Jesus points to
His mighty deeds, which we are accustomed to call His
miracles.
His contemporaries including His disciples narrated
stories about these deeds, which to-day prompt the question:
how are such happenings to be properly assessed and judged?
What really happened in those far-off days? And whatever
be the answer to this question, it is pointed out that we
modern people are in no way furthered thereby. For us,
these miracles do not constitute proof! No, and neither were
they a proof at the time of their taking place; they did not
convince everyone and in fact were rather for many a cause
of offence.
Where Christ holds sway, miraculous things happen, but
the miraculous is not proof in any sense acceptable to the
world; it is only an intimation, which invites decision.
Where Christ reigns, marvellous things happen; and if we
proceed to ask whether this is still the case to-day, we must
be careful not to ask for proofs which might relieve us of the
burden of decision. There are of course no such proofs. It is
often attempted with the best intentions to adduce a proof
of the truth of Christianity by pointing to the enduring effects
